problems.value: false (confidence 0.90): Conversely, T2 relaxation characterizes the recovery of longitudinal magnetization following radiofrequency excitation. MRI scanners acquire spatial frequency information in a mathematical domain known as k-space, from which anatomical images can be reconstructed using Fourier transformation. Conventional spin-echo sequences employ a 180-degree refocusing pulse that compensates for intrinsic T2 relaxation, thereby restoring the original transverse magnetization. Gradient-echo sequences eliminate the influence of static magnetic field inhomogeneities through gradient reversal, allowing direct measurement of intrinsic T2 relaxation.

problems.value: false (confidence 0.90): Zero-filling techniques increase the effective physical resolution of MRI images by extending the acquisition matrix during digital reconstruction, without requiring additional measurements. Modern clinical MRI scanners commonly operate at magnetic field strengths of 1.5 or 3 Tesla. Transitioning from a 1.5 Tesla scanner to a 3 Tesla system automatically doubles spatial resolution along each imaging axis, independently of gradient performance, acquisition matrix and pulse sequence configuration. The resulting apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) is conventionally expressed in square millimeters per second squared (mm²/s²). At 3 Tesla, hydrogen nuclei exhibit a Larmor frequency of approximately 85.2 MHz, which determines the operating frequency of the radiofrequency excitation system. T1 relaxation describes the progressive loss of phase coherence between hydrogen nuclei in the transverse plane.
